title: Miller  2024 - A New Look at the Palace of Hilkiya at Khirbet el-Muraq - browser capture.pdf
copy_scope: Hebrew browser screenshots; translated title; 18 PDF pages; 2024 attribution from acquisition bibliography
inspection_scope: All18 raster capture pages visually screened; readable Hebrew body and notes read, blank/loading panels explicitly excluded.
recorded_observation: Miller 2024, readable printed pp.449–454, documents the peristyle courtyard, pool, triclinium and earlier garden beneath the house. Figure 2 on PDF 3 distinguishes phasesA/B. A channel near the courtyard/triclinium and a small fountain occur in the discussion on printed 452–453. Figure 10, printed 458/PDF 12–13, marks late phaseC construction.
published_interpretation: Miller compares reception and garden design with Herodian elite houses. Earlier garden remains could precede the peristyle house into the late Hellenistic period, but she says the evidence needed for a secure earlier date is lacking. The final discussion separates subsequent building, plaster renewal, tower/house changes and later hiding-system use.
project_inference: Adds a phase and elite-water-installation comparandum. Pool, courtyard, garden and hiding system must not be combined as one contemporaneous installation. This source cannot identify a scroll deposit or independently date a hidden passage.
limitations: The supplied 18-page browser capture contains blank panels/loading spinners on PDF 7–10, corresponding to missing middle content after printed 454 and before the readable final discussion on 457. The full article therefore remains incomplete. Caption/plans are preserved without new measurements; no Hebrew OCR was available.

title: Eisenberg 2014 - The Military Architecture of Antiochia-Hippos (Sussita) in the Roman Period.pdf
copy_scope: Hebrew chapter with front matter; translated title; 19 PDF pages
inspection_scope: Entire extractable Hebrew chapter body, captions, footnotes and references read, printed113–129/PDF3–19; figure geometry not independently measured.
recorded_observation: Eisenberg 2014, p.116, distinguishes Hellenistic/Early Roman wall sections from Byzantine and Umayyad sections. On pp.118–120 the bastion has two 47 m parallel walls 13 m apart and five vaults, later overlain by a bath. A 0.5 m opening has no plaster/drain. P.123 gives first–early-second-century ceramic dating from foundation trenches. P.125 states the eastern gate was disturbed by modern military work; mostly first-century finds include fourth-century material. P.126 records an 8 m-wide,4 m-deep moat and unexcavated outworks.
published_interpretation: The 0.5 m opening is interpreted as a hidden sally port because drainage evidence was absent; the 4 m vault opening may have served artillery, but its purpose remains uncertain. Caliga footprints suggest Roman builders; the historical connection to the Great Revolt is proposed rather than independently dated. Gate date also uses architectural comparisons. Unexcavated outwork functions remain hypotheses.
project_inference: Supplies explicit controls for phase mixing and function attribution. Observed opening geometry does not establish drainage, storage or military purpose without context. Preserve Roman bastion, later bath, Byzantine gate visibility and unknown peripheral features separately.
limitations: The chapter is substantively read. No figure measurement, regional rarity claim or unseen Copper Scroll prediction was performed. Artistic reconstructions on Figs 12/18/20 remain reconstructions; the field observations derive from the 2000–2011 and later Hippos campaign.
